title: State versus Trait Tracker
summary: Simulated experience-sampling data for four fictional people over a fortnight. Students rank them by typical level from a single moment, discover how badly that works, then control within-person variability, measurement error and life events — and watch two people with the same mean turn out to be living quite different fortnights.
learningObjectives: Separate a person's typical level from where they happen to be at one moment.
Explain why within-person variability is a stable characteristic rather than noise to be averaged away.
Explain why measurement error and genuine within-person fluctuation are indistinguishable in one observation and separable across many.
Say how many observations are needed to estimate a person's typical level, and why the answer depends on the person.
Distinguish between-person from within-person variance and interpret the share of variance sitting between people.
privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; every calculation runs in the browser tab, and the tool asks nothing about the person using it.
accessibilityNotes: Ranking uses native selects rather than drag-and-drop; duplicate ranks produce an accessible error. Four-series line charts distinguish people by colour, by dash pattern and by a name printed at the end of each line, and are hidden from assistive technology in favour of visible tables carrying every summary figure. Sliders announce meaningful values ('measurement error standard deviation 3 points'). The random seed is exposed as a number input so a demonstration is exactly reproducible. Keyboard operable throughout; changes announced through the shell's polite live region; reduced motion honoured; forced-colours rules provided; usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
readmeTopic: States versus traits: within-person variability, repeated measurement and what a single administration cannot tell you
simulationNotes: Four fictional people on an arbitrary 0-100 scale with no norms. Each observation is trait + decaying event effect + within-person wobble + measurement error, with wobble drawn from a normal distribution whose SD is a property of the person and error modelled separately so the two can be shown to behave differently under averaging. Randomness uses a seeded mulberry32 generator; the seed is shown and settable, so any dataset is exactly reproducible. Observations are equally spaced with no missingness, no autocorrelation beyond event decay, and no drift in the trait level — all three are unrealistic and are stated as limitations on the page.
